chunks: "I'd treat it in layers. The thing to protect is the gate oxide of the input transistors, which can only take a few volts.
An ESD event is a nanosecond-scale pulse of a couple of amps at kilovolts, so the structure has to shunt that current somewhere harmless, not just limit voltage.
At the pad I put two diodes: one from the pad up to V DD and one from ground up to the pad.
If the pin goes above V DD plus a diode drop, the upper diode steers the current into the supply rail; if it goes below ground minus a diode drop, the lower one conducts.
Those diodes have to be big because they carry amps.
Then a series resistor, a few hundred ohms of poly, drops the remaining voltage and limits current into a smaller secondary clamp right next to the gate.
Between V DD and ground there's a rail clamp, a big NMOS triggered by an RC, which carries the current to the ground pin so the supply doesn't blow up.
On the board I'd add a TVS diode at the connector for IEC-level events and a series resistor, sized so the DC clamp current stays small for overvoltage.
For a 12 volts fault on a 3. 3 volts pin, a 3. 3 kilohms resistor limits the clamp current to about 2. 5 milliamps.
The cost is RC bandwidth and extra capacitance, so I'd check that against signal speed."
